analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 in two steps.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the two-year Congress where it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour to $5.90 about two months after passage, and then to $6.65 a year later. It also would have applied the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, whose workers had long been exempt and could be paid far less, phasing that up gradually. It was introduced on the Senate's first day of business in January 2003 and sent to the committee that handles labor law. The committee never acted on it, and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would have seen their hourly pay rise by up to $1.50 — about 29 percent — over roughly 14 months. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, many employed in its garment and hotel industries, would have gained the most on paper, since local wages there were far below the federal floor.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.90 an hour beginning 60 days after enactment, then to $6.65 an hour one year later [S2] [S3].
Extends the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt, starting at $3.55 there and rising 50 cents every six months until it matches the federal wage [S2] [S3].
A full-time worker at $5.15 earns about $10,700 a year before taxes; the two-step increase to $6.65 would have raised that to roughly $13,800.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail stores, small businesses, and in particular the garment industry of the Northern Mariana Islands, which depended on wages well below the federal floor. Some of the added cost would likely have been passed to consumers through higher prices, and some employers might have cut hours or positions.

drawbacks.text: The increase would have raised labor costs for employers of low-wage workers, especially small restaurants and retailers, and some of that cost typically shows up as higher prices or fewer hours [S3].

Extending the federal wage to the Northern Mariana Islands would have hit its small economy hardest, since its garment factories paid far below the federal minimum; the bill's own text concedes this by phasing the wage in slowly at $3.55 to start [S3].
A 29 percent jump over 14 months is a large, fast increase for businesses operating on thin margins, even if the final wage of $6.65 was modest by later standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to state: millions of the lowest-paid workers would have gotten a meaningful raise, and the gains go overwhelmingly to people at the bottom of the pay scale. The costs fall on their employers and partly on prices, and the Northern Mariana Islands provision needed a long phase-in precisely because the change was disruptive there. On balance this is a well-targeted wage increase, though its speed and the island transition were the honest trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced the first day of the 108th Congress and referred to the Senate's labor committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, so the Senate never got to vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle, the Senate Democratic leader, introduced the bill on January 7, 2003, with 34 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action is recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, and no Senate floor vote appear in the bill's action history for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and bills not passed by then die [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail chains, and small businesses — kept paying the $5.15 federal floor, unchanged since 1997, for the full two years the bill sat untouched. Northern Mariana Islands garment makers kept their lower-wage exemption. Low-wage workers got nothing.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as the chamber's top Democrat; it never advanced past referral.

for.name: 34 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on introduction; all sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership (Chair Judd Gregg)
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 senators behind the bill — the sponsor plus 34 cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the Republican-led Senate never acted on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The largest employer of minimum-wage workers; the bill would have forced a 29 percent raise for its lowest-paid staff over about 14 months. Because it died, the industry kept the $5.15 floor for two more years.
Would have paid higher wages for entry-level staff, with some cost likely passed to consumers. The bill's death spared them the increase.

The island chain was exempt from the federal minimum wage and its garment factories paid far less; the bill would have ended that advantage on a phase-in schedule. This industry's low-wage advantage ran directly against the workers the bill covered.
